metadata.description: An IP network — a prefix, its gateway, and how addresses on it are assigned. The layer 3 half of "which network", independently selectable from the layer 2 segment it usually sits on.

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

ip_family.description: Address family. Derivable from `prefix` and carried anyway ONLY where a provider reports it independently; a value disagreeing with the prefix is drift, not an override.

gateway_address.description: The default route off this subnet, as an address rather than a reference — the address is a property of the subnet, while the device answering it is a `Network.Gateway` and may change without the subnet changing. Absent means no default route (an isolated L3 network).

address_assignment.description: How a host on this subnet gets its address. `pool` means an IPAddressPool within this subnet hands one out and it is reserved before realization — which is what lets an address be held while the workload is still hypothetical (ADR-011).

dns_servers.description: Resolvers offered to hosts on this subnet. Secondary to prefix and gateway (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10 — IPs, gateways and DNS are secondary to segment and performance), carried because a provider reports it with the subnet and a consumer cannot obtain it any other way.

prefix.description: The CIDR actually realized. Where the subnet was ALLOCATED from a larger prefix (the /28-from-a-/16 case), the requested size and the granted range differ, so what a consumer got is a realized fact rather than a restatement of intent.

gateway_address.description: The default route as realized — the address a host on this subnet actually uses.

usable_addresses.description: How many addresses are assignable. DERIVED from the prefix minus the reservations the provider makes (network, broadcast, and whatever the platform holds back — clouds commonly take several), which is why it is an output and not a stored field: only the realizing provider knows its own reservations.

relationships.name: segment
relationships.description: The layer 2 segment this subnet rides on, WHERE THERE IS ONE. Optional and 0..1 on purpose: the L2-to-L3 mapping is not concrete — one segment may carry several subnets, and a cloud provider may expose no segment at all. A consumer selecting a subnet is making a different request from a consumer selecting a segment, and this edge is what relates them without merging them.

relationships.name: network
relationships.description: The logical network (VPC analogue) this subnet belongs to, where the provider exposes one.

adopts.role: The prefix notation and the aggregation semantics — adopted by reference, never re-expressed.

adopts.version: AWS VPC subnet / Azure VNet subnet / GCP subnetwork (convergent de-facto model)
adopts.role: The cloud realization of an L3 network. Recorded so a cloud provider naturalizes into this class rather than a cloud-only branch. The VPC that CONTAINS such a subnet has no class yet, and `contained_by → Network.VirtualNetwork` below is the on-prem attachment-point case rather than a VPC. Tracked separately: a subnet is useful without its container, and guessing the container's shape would be worse than leaving it open.

context.purpose: Give the layer 3 network a first-class identity, so a consumer can require an IP network without naming a segment, and an allocation pool has something to sit inside.
context.plain_description: The IP side of a network — the address range, the way out of it, and how hosts on it get an address. Usually paired with one VLAN, but not always, which is why it is its own thing.
use_when: A workload must land on a particular IP network, whatever segment carries it
An address pool needs an L3 network to belong to
A /28 is allocated from a larger prefix somebody else holds
not_for: The layer 2 segment — that is `Network.VLAN`, and a subnet may not map to exactly one
Handing out individual addresses — that is `Network.IPAddressPool` within this subnet
works_with: `Network.VLAN` — the segment this subnet usually rides on, when there is one
`Network.IPAddressPool` — the allocatable ranges within this subnet
